summary: Carney heads to China to meet Xi, saying Canada could turn to Chinese carmakers if US talks fail, as exports to China jump and October inflation data lands today.
body: Speaking in Cambodia, Prime Minister Mark Carney said a trade deal with the US is still his priority, but that its outcome could lead Canada to seek carmakers from Europe, China or Japan: "It's not leverage. But action, reaction."[^1] Any Chinese investment would have to include real manufacturing, he said, "not just about kit cars."[^1] Since January, Canada has let in up to 49,000 Chinese electric vehicles a year at a 6.1% tariff, a deal Ontario Premier Doug Ford has criticised.[^1] Carney meets Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday morning China time, which is late Monday evening in Ontario, before the APEC summit.[^2]

The trade numbers explain the interest. Statistics Canada figures show exports to China reached $33.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up almost 40%, led by canola, beef, peas and crude oil, while imports from China were about flat at $68.8 billion.[^3] The trade minister's office aims to raise exports to China 50% by 2030; one analyst warns that depending on China "opens us up to leverage and potential coercion."[^3] At the Francophonie summit, Carney also met Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon for the first time since Quebec elected a sovereigntist government; they agreed to hold regular talks.[^4]

At home, Statistics Canada releases October inflation at 8:30 a.m. today. Economists polled by Reuters expect 3.2%, up from 3.1%, well above the Bank of Canada's 2% target.[^5] The Bank raised its rate to 2.5% on Oct. 28 and decides again on Dec. 9; economists disagree on whether businesses will pass higher costs on to shoppers.[^5] For students, this affects prices for food, transit and part-time wages' buying power.
differences: Ottawa sees more trade with China as a way to rely less on the US; critics, including Doug Ford on the EV deal and analyst Vina Nadjibulla, warn it creates new risks.[^1][^3] Desjardins expects inflation to stay high as costs are passed on, while CIBC says profit margins will absorb much of it.[^5]
